newsitem.title: UK: Wall St woes hit Eurobourses; EU summit eyed.
newsitem.headline: Wall St woes hit Eurobourses; EU summit eyed.

text.p: European stock markets slid further in early trading on Friday, prompted by a near 100-point drop on Wall Street, and faced a tense end to the week for the second week running.
Investors, fearing the New York stock market, the world's biggest, might be suffering something more serious than a passing cold, took some more profits after a successful year.
"Institutions have been reluctant to sell the past few weeks but that could change today," one London share dealer said.
Key European bourses lost more than one percent, while Asian markets also weakened but ended above their lows.

On a jittery currency market, the dollar was steady against the mark and lower against the yen. Traders focused on the European Union summit in Dublin, awaiting details of a budgetary stability pact to underpin plans for a single euro currency.
"The market seems pretty relaxed about the summit but I really think there is a lot of confusion," said Peter Von Maydell, senior currency economist at UBS.
"The more the Germans give up their hardline stance, the less damage will be done."
European bond markets were a little shaky as they waited for news from Dublin on how rigorous a stability pact would be.
On Thursday the Dow Jones industrial average of U.S. blue-chip stocks ended down 98.81 points, or 1.54 percent, at 6,303.71 after giving back an early gain of 35 points.
It has fallen 170 points or 2.5 percent in the past two sessions, raising fears that a major correction could be due after gains of almost a third this year.
A week ago markets plunged worldwide after remarks by U.S. central bank chief Alan Greenspan on the "irrational exuberance" of the U.S. stock market.
"The market has been expecting the Dow to come off for sometime now," one senior London share dealer said.
"We're bound to follow it lower. But since we didn't go up as much this year, we shouldn't have as hard a landing." London's FTSE 100 index has risen around nine percent this year.
German shares also tracked Wall Street lower and some Frankfurt dealers feared worse to come.
"After all, it's Friday the 13th," said one dealer. "I am sure there are more people out there who will come in later and sell."

In the latest news in a long-running corporate saga, German prosecutors said they had filed criminal charges against four former General Motors executives who allegedly stole secret documents when they quit the U.S. carmaker to join rival Volkswagen. VW shares were little changed.
The Paris bourse's blue-chip CAC-40 index opened well down in active trading, hit by falls in markets elsewhere.
"People are getting more and more nervous about Wall Street," said Olivier Blitz, chief salesman at Paris brokerage IFF.
In Tokyo, the 225-issue Nikkei average dropped more than 500 points before recovering by the close. It ended down 159.81 points, or 0.78 percent, at 20,341.39.
On the foreign exchanges, Wall Street's change of heart overnight had minimal effect on the dollar.
Market participants increasingly see year-end profit-taking as a more important cause of weakness in U.S. asset markets than any deep change in longer-term valuations, analysts said.
The peseta was virtually unchanged at 84.24 to the mark, versus Thursday's late 84.23, after the Bank of Spain cut its key money rate to 6.25 percent from 6.75, the seventh cut of the year.
CURRENCIES AT 1015 GMT
The dollar was quoted around 113.05 yen and 1.5440 marks against 113.33 and 1.5427 in late European business on Thursday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1015 GMT
The FTSE 100 index of leading British shares was down 43.7 points at 3,947.0.
The 30-share DAX index in Frankfurt shed 36.19 to 2,810.89.
In Paris, the CAC-40 index was 26.08 lower at 2,186.03.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold rose to $369.25 an ounce from Thursday's London close of $368.45. Silver edged up to $4.84 from $4.82.
